claim: Cofilin is a member of the actin-depolymerizing factor/cofilin (ADF/cofilin) family that is present in all eukaryotes.
source: Cofilin is a member of the actin-depolymerizing factor/cofilin (ADF/cofilin) family that is present in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cofilin classification and distribution.

claim: There are two major isoforms of cofilin in mammals: cofilin 1 and cofilin 2, predominantly found in non-muscle and muscle tissues, respectively.
source: There are two major isoforms of cofilin in mammals: cofilin 1 and cofilin 2, predominantly found in non-muscle and muscle tissues, respectively (Bamburg and Bernstein, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bamburg and Bernstein, 2010.

claim: Cofilin promotes the depolymerization and severing of actin filaments in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Cofilin promotes the depolymerization and severing of actin filaments in a concentration-dependent manner (Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006.

claim: Cofilin collaborates or competes with other actin binding proteins (ABPs) in the process of actin filament dynamics.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The structure of an actin filament has traditionally been represented as a simplistic atomic model derived from the G-actin structure in the Holmes model without considering conformational changes occurring within each protomer during actin polymerization.
source: The structure of an actin filament has traditionally been represented as a simplistic atomic model derived from the G-actin structure in the Holmes model (Holmes et al., 1990) without considering the conformational changes occurring within each protomer during actin polymerization (Kasai et al., 1962; Rich and Estes, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 1990, Kasai et al., 1962, and Rich and Estes, 1976.

claim: The rigid-body rotation of the G-actin crystal structure used in the Holmes model prompted the development of accurate models that consider structural changes within protomers, such as the X-ray diffraction Lorenz model and Oda model.
source: The rigid-body rotation of the G-actin crystal structure used in the Holmes model prompted the development of accurate models that consider structural changes within protomers, such as the X-ray diffraction Lorenz model (Lorenz et al., 1993) and Oda model (Oda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lorenz et al., 1993 and Oda et al., 2009.

claim: The actin protomer consists of two domains, the inner domain (ID) and the outer domain (OD), with relatively limited contact between them.
source: The actin protomer consists of two domains, the inner domain (ID) and the outer domain (OD), with relatively limited contact between them.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about actin.

claim: The polypeptide chain traverses between the inner and outer domains twice: at the loop centered around residue Lys336 and at the linker helix Gln137-Ser145.
source: The polypeptide chain traverses between these domains twice: at the loop centered around residue Lys336 and at the linker helix Gln137-Ser145, which functions as the axis of a hinge between the domains.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about actin.

claim: Two clefts are formed between the inner and outer domains of actin.
source: As a result, two clefts are formed between these domains (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dominguez and Holmes, 2011.

claim: The upper cleft, located between subdomain (SD2) and SD4, serves as a binding site for nucleotides and divalent ions like Mg2+.
source: The upper cleft, located between subdomain (SD2) and SD4, serves as a binding site for nucleotides and divalent ions like Mg2+.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about actin.

claim: The lower cleft, located between SD1 and SD3, is characterized by predominantly hydrophobic residues and serves as the primary binding site for most ABPs including cofilin.
source: On the other hand, the lower cleft, located between SD1 and SD3, is characterized by residues Tyr143, Ala144, Gly146, Thr148, Gly168, Ile341, Ile345, Leu346, Leu349, Thr351, and Met355, which are predominantly hydrophobic. This cleft serves as the primary binding site for most ABPs including cofilin and is also responsible for critical longitudinal contacts between actin protomers within the filament (Dominguez, 2004; Fujii et al., 2010; Oda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dominguez, 2004, Fujii et al., 2010, and Oda et al., 2009.

claim: The actin filament is a double-stranded helical structure formed by the crossover of two long-pitch helices.
source: The actin filament is a double-stranded helical structure formed by the crossover of two long-pitch helices
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about actin filaments.

claim: The distance between the crossover points in actin filaments is known as the half helical pitch (HHP), which is approximately 36 nm.
source: the distance between the crossover points is known as the half helical pitch (HHP), which is approximately 36 nm (Fujii et al., 2010; Holmes et al., 1990; Lorenz et al., 1993; Oda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A canonical half helix is composed of 13 actin protomers (6.5 protomer pairs).
source: A canonical half helix is composed of 13 actin protomers (6.5 protomer pairs).

claim: When cofilin binds and sits on the sides of SD1 and SD2 of two adjacent actin protomers, the OD (SD1, SD2) in bound protomers becomes more twisted (a decrease in PC2), but without significantly affecting the closing of the nucleotide binding cleft (nearly unchanging PC1).
source: When cofilin binds and sits on the sides of SD1 and SD2 of two adjacent actin protomers (Figure 2B and C), the OD (SD1, SD2) in bound protomers becomes more twisted (a decrease in PC2), but without significantly affecting the closing of the nucleotide binding cleft (nearly unchanging PC1).
evidence: This claim is based on PCA analysis results and structural interpretation shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: The transition from the C-actin to breaking the filament into monomer G-actin structure additionally requires the opening of the nucleotide binding cleft (decreasing PC1).
source: The transition from the C-actin to breaking the filament into monomer G-actin structure additionally requires the opening of the nucleotide binding cleft (decreasing PC1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA analysis results.

claim: The bridging between two protomers by cofilin can compensate for all the losses in the disrupted interactions between the SD2 D-loop and SD1 pocket.
source: However, this process is normally hindered in the presence of cofilin, as the bridging between two protomers can compensate for all the losses in the disrupted interactions between the SD2 D-loop and SD1 pocket (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural analysis shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: Cofilin clusters can convert bare protomers within the shortened bare half helices on the PE side into C-actin-like structures.
source: Strikingly, the HS-AFM results suggest that cofilin clusters can convert bare protomers within the shortened bare half helices on the PE side into C-actin-like structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on HS-AFM observations.

claim: Unless additional cofilin molecules quickly bind to the protomers with C-actin-like structures on the PE side, the disrupted interactions would readily lead to the nucleotide binding cleft transitioning from the closed to open states, resembling C-actin to G-actin transition.
source: Unless additional cofilin molecules quickly bind to the protomers with C-actin-like structures on the PE side, the disrupted interactions would readily lead to the nucleotide binding cleft transitioning from the closed to open states, resembling C-actin to G-actin transition (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the PCA and HS-AFM results.

claim: The proposed hypothesis regarding the shift from C-actin-like structure to G-actin aligns with earlier studies suggesting that the binding sites of cofilin encompass a region that overlaps with G-actin structure.
source: Our proposed hypothesis regarding the shift from C-actin-like structure to G-actin aligns with earlier studies suggesting that the binding sites of cofilin encompass a region that overlaps with G-actin structure (Carlier et al., 1997; Mannherz et al., 2007; Narita, 2020; Tanaka et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dissociation of the D-loop from an adjacent actin subunit directly causes the transition to the G-form of actin, which is regarded as the most stable configuration for the actin molecule.
source: The dissociation of the D-loop from an adjacent actin subunit directly causes the transition to the G-form of actin, which is regarded as the most stable configuration for the actin molecule (Oda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oda et al., 2019.

claim: The protomers within the shortened bare half helix near a cofilin cluster on the PE side of F-ADP.Pi-actin may be quickly converted to F-ADP-actin and C-actin-like structure through F-actin to C-actin transition.
source: Additionally, the protomers within the shortened bare half helix near a cofilin cluster on the PE side of F-ADP.Pi-actin may be quickly converted to F-ADP-actin and C-actin-like structure through F-actin to C-actin transition.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: This explains the preferential binding of cofilin to ADP-actin on the PE side and why filament breakages are more commonly observed at or near the boundary of cofilactin and bare actin on the PE side, rather than where actin protomers are fully bound with cofilin.
source: Together, this explains the preferential binding of cofilin to ADP-actin on the PE side and why filament breakages are more commonly observed at or near the boundary of cofilactin and bare actin on the PE side, rather than where actin protomers are fully bound with cofilin (Bibeau et al., 2021; Ngo et al., 2015; Suarez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reduction in torsional flexibility associated with variable helical twists, rather than the large conformational change in F-actin's protomers linked to ATP hydrolysis, accounts for the inhibition of cofilin binding by Pi.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the reduction in torsional flexibility associated with variable helical twists, rather than the large conformational change in F-actin's protomers linked to ATP hydrolysis, accounts for the inhibition of cofilin binding by Pi (Figure 10H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations shown in Figure 10H.

claim: The absence of bound Pi possibly increases the torsional flexibilities during helical twisting of ADP-bound actin filaments in contrast to their ADP.Pi-bound counterparts.
source: We suggest that the absence of bound Pi possibly increases the torsional flexibilities during helical twisting of ADP-bound actin filaments in contrast to their ADP.Pi-bound counterparts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Actin structure-dependent preferential binding of actin-binding proteins (ABPs) have been investigated at the molecular and cellular levels.
source: Actin structure-dependent preferential binding of actin-binding proteins (ABPs) have been investigated at the molecular and cellular levels (Hayakawa et al., 2023; Jegou and Romet-Lemonne, 2020; Jégou and Romet-Lemonne, 2016; Ngo et al., 2016; Tokuraku et al., 2020; Tokuraku et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Harris and colleagues reported biased localization of tandem calponin homology domains (CH1-CH2) that can be mutated to selectively bind different actin conformations at the leading or trailing edge of motile cells.
source: Notably, Harris and colleagues reported biased localization of tandem calponin homology domains (CH1-CH2) that can be mutated to selectively bind different actin conformations at the leading or trailing edge of motile cells (Harris et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2020.

claim: The untwisting of the long-pitch helix of the actin filament induced by diaphanous-related formin mDia1 inhibits cofilin binding.
source: The untwisting of the long-pitch helix of the actin filament induced by diaphanous-related formin mDia1 inhibits cofilin binding (Mizuno et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mizuno et al., 2018.

claim: Stretching actin filaments within cells enhances their binding affinities for the myosin II motor domain.
source: Stretching actin filaments within cells enhances their binding affinities for the myosin II motor domain (Uyeda et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uyeda et al., 2011.
